studies.title: People with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia accumulate chronic physical illness decades early — and young women fare worst
studies.ns_score_reason: enormous, population-wide cohort with a genuinely startling age-and-sex gradient; limited by hospital-registry data and no lived-experience input.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers tracked 178,665 people in Queensland, Australia, through statewide hospital registries from 2000 to 2023 — 30,189 with schizophrenia-spectrum or bipolar-spectrum disorders (median age 32) matched 4:1 to hospital patients without them. They counted not single illnesses but how many separate *body systems* had developed chronic disease. The gap widened the more systems were involved: adjusted hazard ratios rose from 1.85 for one affected system to 3.16 for five or more, and among women under 25 the hazard ratio for five-system multimorbidity reached 9.24.
studies.why_it_matters: The familiar statistic is that severe mental illness shortens life by 15–20 years; this quantifies the machinery behind it, showing disease accumulating across multiple organ systems from young adulthood rather than clustering in later life.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive hook is that the youngest patients show the largest excess, not the oldest — a 23-year-old woman recently diagnosed with bipolar disorder is at nine times the risk of having five body systems affected within 20 years. Open on the moment of first psychiatric admission as an under-recognized moment of physical-health triage. Call Sean Halstead and Dan Siskind at the University of Queensland; Toby Pillinger at King's College London for outside comment.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health-policy or general-interest outlet on the structural reasons psychiatric patients fall out of physical medicine — "diagnostic overshadowing," fragmented services, and what integrated young-adult clinics in Denmark and Finland are trying instead.
studies.caveats: Observational design (cannot establish causation); hospital registry data means the comparison group is also hospital patients, likely underestimating the gap versus the general population; no ethnicity data; medication effects not disentangled from illness effects; several co-authors report extensive pharmaceutical industry ties (study itself unfunded).

studies.title: Lithium's reputation as the anti-suicide drug does not hold up against valproate
studies.ns_score_reason: directly challenges a strongly held clinical belief with both new cohort data and a network meta-analysis; limited by observational confounding and low event numbers.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Using 20 years of Hong Kong Hospital Authority records, researchers compared 1,379 people with bipolar disorder who started lithium monotherapy with 5,556 who started valproate, balancing the groups statistically. There was no significant difference in suicide risk (weighted HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.54–1.08). A network meta-analysis pooling 12 observational studies and 3 trials reached the same conclusion: both drugs beat no treatment (lithium HR 0.46; valproate HR 0.63), but neither beat the other.
studies.why_it_matters: Lithium is widely described as uniquely protective against suicide, a claim that shapes prescribing for a drug with demanding monitoring and real toxicity. This suggests the anti-suicide effect may be a mood-stabilization effect rather than something special about lithium — though observational data cannot settle it.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the deflation: one of psychiatry's most-repeated claims — "lithium is the only drug shown to reduce suicide" — survives as "mood stabilizers reduce suicide." Open on the clinical dilemma faced by a patient weighing lithium's blood tests and thyroid risks against valproate. Call Francisco T. T. Lai at the University of Hong Kong; worth pairing with a UK lithium researcher such as Joseph Hayes at UCL for the counterargument.
studies.wider_angle: A specialist-outlet piece on why definitive head-to-head trials of old, off-patent psychiatric drugs almost never get funded — the meta-analysis here couldn't even pool its three RCTs because they were methodologically incompatible.
studies.caveats: Observational design (cannot establish causation); confounding by indication is near-certain, as lithium tends to be given to different patients than valproate; suicide is a rare outcome so confidence intervals are wide; single-territory cohort with prescribing patterns that may not generalize; meta-analytic component rests almost entirely on observational studies.

studies.title: Walking more lifts your mood, and your mood gets you walking — but screen time only pushes one way
studies.ns_score_reason: an intensively sampled, passively sensed within-person design that separates cause-candidates from correlations; limited by modest N and small effect sizes.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Over 14 days, 128 people (mean age 37.8; 82 of them offspring of a parent with bipolar disorder) reported positive and negative affect five times daily while their phones passively logged step counts and screen-on time. Using dynamic structural equation modeling, positive affect and step count fed each other bidirectionally; higher positive affect predicted *less* subsequent screen time, and more screen time predicted subsequent negative affect. Negative affect, strikingly, predicted nothing at all. Familial risk didn't change these dynamics — it just shifted everyone's baseline mood down.
studies.why_it_matters: The asymmetry is the story: good mood appears to be the engine of the behavior–feeling loop, while bad mood is largely a passenger — which cuts against the intuition that low mood is what drives people to the sofa and the phone.
studies.pitch_angle: Everyone assumes feeling bad is what makes you scroll. In this data, feeling *good* is what makes you put the phone down and go outside — and the loop runs identically whether or not you carry familial risk for bipolar disorder. Open on a participant's ordinary Tuesday as reconstructed from five mood pings and a step counter. Call Sarah Sperry at the University of Michigan or Manon Hillegers at Erasmus MC.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a psychology or technology outlet on what "passive sensing" studies are quietly revealing about screen time — that the effects are real but tiny, and that the interesting question has shifted from how much people use their phones to what mood state they are in when they pick them up.
studies.caveats: Small N (128) with only 32 participants having any mood-disorder history and just 3 with recurrent disorder, so the risk-moderation null is underpowered; self-reported affect; effect sizes are very small (β ≈ 0.03–0.07); screen-on time doesn't capture what people were doing; 14-day follow-up only; Dutch cohort.

studies.title: Brain blood flow is lowest in bipolar disorder with psychosis — and higher flow tracks worse symptoms
studies.ns_score_reason: very large multi-site imaging sample and a neat dissociation between diagnosis and symptom severity; limited by small bipolar subgroup and null cognitive findings.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled arterial spin labeling scans — an MRI method that measures blood flow without injected tracer — from 2,412 people with schizophrenia, 2,278 with schizoaffective disorder, 158 with psychotic bipolar disorder and 401 neurotypical controls, mapping resting cerebral blood flow across 60 brain regions. People with psychotic bipolar disorder showed the most pronounced reduction in gray matter blood flow (d = −0.259), with hypoperfusion across 25 regions. Yet *within* patients, higher overall blood flow correlated with worse psychotic symptoms, and hyperperfusion of the right superior temporal sulcus tracked psychotic, manic and depressive symptoms alike.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding splits trait from state — chronically low perfusion may mark who has the disorder, while transient overactivity may mark how ill they are right now — and supports efforts to sort psychosis by biology rather than by DSM label.
studies.pitch_angle: Diagnosis by category barely predicted brain perfusion; a "biotype" derived from neurophysiology did. Lead on the awkward fact that the bipolar group, usually thought of as the milder end of the psychosis spectrum, had the largest perfusion deficit. Call Paulo Lizano at Beth Israel Deaconess, and Carol Tamminga at UT Southwestern for the biotype framework.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature for a neuroscience or medical outlet on the decade-long attempt to replace psychiatric diagnoses with biomarker-defined "biotypes" — what B-SNIP has and hasn't delivered, and why no brain measure has yet made it into a clinic.
studies.caveats: Observational design; the bipolar group (n=158) is far smaller than the schizophrenia groups, so the largest effect rests on the smallest sample; cross-sectional, so trait-versus-state interpretation is inferred, not demonstrated; medication effects on cerebral blood flow are a known confound and hard to exclude; no CBF–cognition associations survived correction.

studies.title: Long-acting antipsychotic injections help some people with intellectual disability — and may be harming those prescribed them off-label
studies.ns_score_reason: a clever within-person design answering a question almost no trial has touched, with a genuinely divergent result for off-label use.
studies.the_study: Using 20 years of Hong Kong health records, researchers identified 1,675 adults with intellectual disability who had been on both long-acting injectable and oral antipsychotics at different times, and compared each person to themselves. Among those with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, injections were linked to fewer hospitalizations and dramatically fewer extrapyramidal side effects (IRR 0.34), though more cardiovascular admissions. Among those *without* such a diagnosis — where the drugs are prescribed off-label, typically for challenging behavior — injections were associated with *more* all-cause and somatic hospitalizations and no benefit for behavior problems.
studies.why_it_matters: Antipsychotics are prescribed to a large fraction of people with intellectual disability who have no psychotic illness, a practice campaigners have challenged for years with little hard outcome data; this provides some.
studies.pitch_angle: The same drug, the same people, opposite outcomes depending on why it was prescribed. Open on the scale of off-label antipsychotic use in intellectual disability services and what "deprescribing" would actually involve. Call Esther Chan at the University of Hong Kong, and Shoumitro Deb at Imperial College London, a long-standing critic of overprescribing in this population.
studies.wider_angle: An investigative or policy piece for a UK health outlet revisiting the STOMP program — the decade-old NHS drive to stop overmedicating people with learning disabilities and autism — and whether prescribing has actually fallen.
studies.caveats: Observational design and self-controlled case series cannot rule out that people were switched to injections precisely when they were deteriorating; single territory; off-label subgroup may differ systematically in ways within-person design cannot fix; several authors declare extensive pharmaceutical funding including from manufacturers of long-acting injectables.

studies.title: The body's own cannabis-like chemicals fall as mania lifts — unless the person uses cannabis
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean longitudinal within-patient design and a plausible biological story about why cannabis complicates bipolar recovery, but only 23 patients.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Twenty-three people with bipolar I disorder had blood drawn during an acute manic episode and again after clinical stabilization, with the endocannabinoids anandamide and 2-AG measured by mass spectrometry. In non-users of cannabis, both molecules fell significantly as mania resolved. In cannabis users, levels stayed flat despite equivalent clinical improvement — and endocannabinoid levels didn't track symptom severity scores in either group.
studies.why_it_matters: It hints that recovery from mania involves a biochemical reset that cannabis use blocks, offering a candidate mechanism for the well-documented but poorly explained link between cannabis and worse bipolar outcomes. Early stage — a hypothesis worth testing, not a clinical finding.
studies.pitch_angle: Two patients leave the ward looking equally well; only one of them has biochemically returned to baseline. Lead on the gap between feeling better and being better. Call Isabella Pacchiarotti or Eduard Vieta at Hospital Clínic de Barcelona; Michael Berk at Deakin for the broader bipolar-biomarker view.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a science or drug-policy outlet on the endocannabinoid system as a mood regulator — a signaling network discovered only because researchers went looking for what cannabis binds to, and which is now implicated in everything from appetite to stress recovery.
studies.caveats: Small N (23); no healthy control group sampled in parallel; cannabis use self-reported and group sizes not stated; plasma endocannabinoids are an indirect proxy for brain signaling; medication changes between the two timepoints are an obvious confound; multiple authors report extensive pharmaceutical industry payments.

studies.title: People with serious mental illness want AI companions — but only ones built with them, not for them
studies.ns_score_reason: rare first-person data from a group usually discussed rather than consulted, and an irresistible quote; limited by qualitative secondary analysis and an author's commercial stake.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers reanalyzed three focus groups held across supportive housing facilities in New York City with residents living with schizophrenia-spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder or major depression. Participants were simultaneously enthusiastic and wary: they valued AI for reminders, daily functioning and simple companionship — one said "if no one told you I love you today, you have someone that cares for you" — while raising pointed concerns about data misuse, overreliance and losing their own critical thinking. Trust rose specifically when tools were personalized and co-designed with people who have lived experience.
studies.why_it_matters: Companion chatbots are being pushed hardest at exactly the people most likely to be isolated and least likely to be consulted about the design; this is a rare case of asking them directly.
studies.pitch_angle: The quote in the title is the hook, and the surprise is how sophisticated the skepticism is — these are not naive users, they're worried about surveillance and about outsourcing their own judgment. Open on a resident in supportive housing weighing loneliness against privacy. Call Karen Fortuna at Dartmouth's Patient Innovation Lab — and note upfront that she holds equity in a companion-AI company.
studies.wider_angle: A reported feature for a technology or social-affairs outlet on the emerging market in AI companionship for isolated populations — who is buying it, whether it substitutes for staffed human support, and what regulators are doing about apps that say "I care about you."
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (three focus groups, N not reported); secondary analysis of data gathered for another purpose; single city and single housing-model population may not generalize; senior author holds an equity interest in Companion, Inc.; no outcome data whatsoever — this is perceptions only.

studies.title: A blood test may show whether lithium is reaching someone's brain
studies.ns_score_reason: an appealing proof-of-concept linking gene activity in blood to brain structure, but cross-sectional and non-randomized.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In 116 people experiencing a depressive episode within bipolar disorder, researchers compared gene expression in circulating immune cells between those on long-term lithium and those not, then linked that expression to diffusion MRI measures of white matter. Five genes differed (SEPTIN11, DGKK and TPPP3 up; LEF1-AS1 and PLXDC1 down), and crucially the relationship between those genes' activity and white matter microstructure existed *only* in lithium-treated patients.
studies.why_it_matters: Lithium works well for some people and not others, and there is currently no way to tell early which is which. A peripheral transcriptomic signature that tracks brain white matter would be a step toward a blood-based readout of the drug's biological effect — though it is nowhere near a clinical test.
studies.pitch_angle: Seventy-plus years after lithium entered psychiatry, nobody can say why it works or predict who it will help. Lead on that embarrassment, then on the idea of reading the drug's brain effects from a blood sample. Call Francesco Benedetti and Sara Poletti at San Raffaele in Milan.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a chemistry or history-of-medicine outlet on lithium itself — the cheapest, oldest, most effective and least understood drug in psychiatry, now also a strategic mineral, and increasingly hard to persuade young psychiatrists to prescribe.
studies.caveats: Observational and cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); lithium-treated and untreated patients were not randomized, so the groups likely differ in illness course and other medications; single center; modest N for a transcriptomics study; no replication cohort; gene expression in blood is an indirect proxy for brain biology.

studies.title: Half of people with anorexia or bulimia also meet criteria for a personality disorder — but almost nothing is known about why
studies.ns_score_reason: a rigorous credibility audit of an entire literature with a striking negative verdict, but it's a review of reviews with no new data.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: An umbrella review pulled together 61 meta-analyses yielding 213 estimates on what co-occurs with anorexia, bulimia and binge-eating disorder, then re-pooled the data and graded how trustworthy each estimate was. Prevalence figures held up reasonably well — any personality disorder in 49% of anorexia and 54% of bulimia cases, non-suicidal self-injury in 37% of bulimia, tobacco use disorder in 47.7% of binge-eating disorder, bipolar disorder in 9.1% of binge-eating disorder. But not a single estimate of a *risk factor* or *outcome* reached convincing or even highly suggestive credibility.
studies.why_it_matters: It draws a sharp line between what the eating-disorder literature can claim (these conditions travel together) and what it cannot (which causes which, or what happens next) — a distinction routinely blurred in both clinical guidance and coverage.
studies.pitch_angle: After decades of research and hundreds of meta-analytic estimates, we can say what co-occurs with eating disorders and essentially nothing about why or what follows. Lead on that gap and what it means for someone being assessed today. Call Michele Fornaro at Federico II University of Naples.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-focused piece for a specialist or academic-audience outlet on umbrella reviews as an accountability tool — the growing practice of grading whole evidence bases and how often headline findings turn out to be "weak credibility."
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of existing meta-analyses of observational studies — inherits every bias in the source literature; restricted to three eating-disorder diagnoses, excluding ARFID and others; prevalence estimates carry very wide intervals (bipolar disorder in BED: 3–23%); no causal inference possible.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- The diagnostic-category problem recurs. Last run, "Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia look identical in blood tests at the first psychotic episode" (PMID 42112712) and "Memory circuits go wrong in different ways in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder" (PMID 42679550) both probed whether biology respects DSM boundaries. This run, "Brain blood flow is lowest in bipolar disorder with psychosis — and higher flow tracks worse symptoms" (PMID 42779463) lands on the same fault line from a much larger imaging sample, and with an added twist: the perfusion deficit was largest in the smallest, supposedly mildest group.
- The "tidy evidence, messy patient" thread continues. The trial-eligibility study from Naples (PMID 42575197) is echoed by the same senior author's umbrella review this run, "Half of people with anorexia or bulimia also meet criteria for a personality disorder — but almost nothing is known about why" (PMID 42777340), which finds that not one risk-factor or outcome estimate in an entire comorbidity literature reaches convincing credibility.
- Long-acting injectable antipsychotics get a second, better-powered look. "Loading the dose of a long-acting antipsychotic injection upfront shortens hospital stays for women" (PMID 41924987, N=87, retrospective) is followed by "Long-acting antipsychotic injections help some people with intellectual disability — and may be harming those prescribed them off-label" (PMID 42711066), a within-person analysis of 1,675 people over 20 years — a substantial step up in design quality on the same drug class.

**Advances**
- Biomarker ambition has shifted from crude to targeted. Last run's negative result on routine blood counts (PMID 42112712) is answered this run by "A blood test may show whether lithium is reaching someone's brain" (PMID 42742966), which links peripheral gene expression to white matter microstructure — a more specific, though still preliminary, version of the same "read the brain from blood" idea.
- The overturning genre recurs with a bigger target. "Serotonin abnormality blamed on borderline personality disorder turns out to belong to depression" (PMID 42173043) reattributed one biomarker; "Lithium's reputation as the anti-suicide drug does not hold up against valproate" (PMID 42765379) questions one of psychiatry's most-repeated prescribing claims, using both a Hong Kong cohort and a network meta-analysis.

**Counterpoints**
- Two explanations for the cannabis–bipolar link now sit side by side. "Genes for addiction — not for drinking or smoking as such — explain why bipolar disorder and substance problems travel together" (PMID 42636965) located the overlap in inherited dependence liability; "The body's own cannabis-like chemicals fall as mania lifts — unless the person uses cannabis" (PMID 42735776) proposes a state-level biochemical mechanism instead. Neither rules the other out, and the pairing is a ready-made piece on trait versus state accounts of comorbidity.

**New themes**
- Physical multimorbidity arrives as a topic in its own right with "People with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia accumulate chronic physical illness decades early — and young women fare worst" (PMID 42586082); nothing in the previous digest addressed bodily disease burden directly.
- The digital thread has moved from prediction to sensing and companionship: last run's algorithm bake-off (PMID 42600789) is replaced by passive phone sensing of mood and steps (PMID 42765378) and by first-person views on AI companions from people in supportive housing (PMID 42789145).
- Off-label prescribing in intellectual disability (PMID 42711066) is a new population for this topic and opens onto the UK's STOMP program.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Three studies in this batch describe what happens to the bodies of people with serious mental illness, and the picture is worse and starts earlier than the standard "15–20 years of life lost" line implies. The Queensland cohort found chronic disease accumulating across five or more organ systems from young adulthood, with a hazard ratio of 9.24 in women under 25 (PMID 42586082); the Hong Kong within-person study found that antipsychotic injections prescribed off-label for challenging behavior in intellectual disability were followed by *more* somatic hospitalizations with no behavioral benefit, and that even on-label use raised cardiovascular admissions (PMID 42711066); and the lithium-versus-valproate analysis removes the main justification for accepting lithium's thyroid and renal monitoring burden — its supposedly unique anti-suicide effect — in favor of no difference (PMID 42765379). The passive-sensing study adds the one lever that points the other way: positive mood and step counts feed each other, while low mood predicts nothing (PMID 42765378).

**Why pitch this now:** The physical-health penalty of severe mental illness is usually reported as a single mortality statistic; this batch breaks it into organ systems, ages, prescribing decisions and a plausible behavioral entry point, all within a month, and it does so as regulators and services in the UK and Australia are being pressed on deprescribing and on integrated young-adult clinics.

**Angle:** Follow the physical body through a psychiatric career — first admission at 23 as an unrecognized moment of medical triage, the mood stabilizer chosen partly on a claim that may not hold, the injection given for behavior rather than illness, and the modest, real gains available from simply moving more. Aimed at a general science-literate readership interested in how medicine divides the mind from the rest of the patient.

**Potential headlines:**
- Chronic illness starts stacking up in bipolar patients in their twenties, not their fifties
- The riskiest patients on the psychiatric ward are the youngest ones
- What a psychiatric diagnosis quietly predicts about your heart, kidneys and lungs

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — has the length for a four-strand piece and an audience already following mortality-gap and deprescribing stories in mental health.
- **The Guardian science desk** — the intellectual-disability prescribing strand connects directly to STOMP and to ongoing UK reporting on overmedication in learning disability services.
- **STAT** — the lithium-versus-valproate deflation and the injectable-antipsychotic harm signal sit squarely in their prescribing and drug-safety beat.
- **Undark** — suited to the structural framing of diagnostic overshadowing and why psychiatric patients drop out of physical medicine.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Bipolar — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-27 | **Studies reviewed:** 9
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-27

---

### Study 1: People with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia accumulate chronic physical illness decades early — and young women fare worst
**PMID:** 42586082 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers check out: 178,665 total, 30,189 cases, median age 32, 1:4 matching, aHRs 1.85 → 3.16, female <25 with ≥5 systems aHR 9.24, no lived-experience involvement, no funding, ethnicity data unavailable. Caveats are well matched to the abstract.

**Issue A. Suggested "outside comment" source is a study co-author** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Call Sean Halstead and Dan Siskind at the University of Queensland; Toby Pillinger at King's College London for outside comment."
- **Abstract says:** Author list includes "Pillinger T(10)" — "Department of Psychosis Studies, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, King's College London."
- **Problem:** Pillinger is a co-author of this paper, so he cannot serve as an independent voice on it. A writer working from this digest would burn a call and look unprepared.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Sean Halstead and Dan Siskind at the University of Queensland (lead and senior authors); note Toby Pillinger at King's College London is also a co-author — for genuinely independent comment, approach a cardiometabolic-psychiatry researcher not on the author list."

**Issue B. Pitch conflates a hazard ratio with an absolute 20-year risk, and a combined SMI group with bipolar disorder** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a 23-year-old woman recently diagnosed with bipolar disorder is at nine times the risk of having five body systems affected within 20 years"
- **Abstract says:** "the highest observed in females younger than 25 years with at least five affected systems (adjusted subdistribution HR 9·24 [95% CI 7·30–11·71])" — with the 20-year figures being separate absolute cumulative incidence differences (11·66 additional cases per 100 persons for ≥5 systems).
- **Problem:** Two splices. The 9.24 is a relative hazard over the whole follow-up, not a 20-year risk; and it applies to the pooled schizophrenia-spectrum *or* bipolar-spectrum group, not to bipolar disorder specifically.
- **Suggested fix:** "a woman diagnosed with a schizophrenia- or bipolar-spectrum disorder before 25 has roughly nine times the hazard of accumulating chronic disease in five or more body systems; in absolute terms the group gained about 12 extra such cases per 100 people over 20 years"

---

### Study 2: Lithium's reputation as the anti-suicide drug does not hold up against valproate
**PMID:** 42765379 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Cohort numbers (1,379 lithium; 5,556 valproate), weighted HR 0.76 (0.54–1.08), network HRs 0.46 and 0.63, and the non-significant lithium-vs-valproate comparison are all accurate. NS fit of 7 is defensible — this is a large IPTW-weighted registry cohort, not small or self-reported.

**Issue A. Misstates what the network meta-analysis pooled** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "A network meta-analysis pooling 12 observational studies and 3 trials reached the same conclusion"
- **Abstract says:** "The meta-analysis identified 3 RCTs and 12 observational studies. Meta-analysis of RCTs was precluded due to methodological incompatibilities. Pairwise meta-analysis of eight observational studies showed no significant difference..."
- **Problem:** The three RCTs were explicitly *not* pooled, and the pairwise synthesis used eight, not twelve, observational studies. The digest's own "wider angle" contradicts the body text on exactly this point ("couldn't even pool its three RCTs").
- **Suggested fix:** "A network meta-analysis drawing on the identified observational literature — the three RCTs were too methodologically incompatible to pool — reached the same conclusion"

**Issue B. Pitch presents a one-sided safety trade-off** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open on the clinical dilemma faced by a patient weighing lithium's blood tests and thyroid risks against valproate."
- **Abstract says:** "The choice between these two mood stabilizers should be guided by individual patient characteristics and safety considerations."
- **Problem:** The framing lists lithium's burdens only, implying valproate is the easier option. Valproate carries its own well-established safety constraints (notably in people who can become pregnant), and the abstract's conclusion turns explicitly on safety considerations for both drugs.
- **Suggested fix:** "Open on the clinical dilemma: lithium's monitoring burden and thyroid risk on one side, valproate's own safety restrictions on the other — with efficacy against suicide no longer the tiebreaker."

---

### Study 3: Walking more lifts your mood, and your mood gets you walking — but screen time only pushes one way
**PMID:** 42765378 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=128, mean age 37.8, 82 bipolar offspring, 32 with mood-disorder history (3 recurrent), 14 days, five pings daily, DSEM, all betas and directions verified against the abstract.

**Issue A. "Everyone's" baseline mood misattributes the group difference** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Familial risk didn't change these dynamics — it just shifted everyone's baseline mood down."
- **Abstract says:** "Familial risk status and recurrent mood disorders did not alter these bidirectional effects, but were associated with lower PA and higher NA on average."
- **Problem:** The shift applies to the at-risk participants relative to controls, not to "everyone." As written it reads as though the whole sample's mood dropped.
- **Suggested fix:** "Familial risk didn't change these dynamics — those at risk simply ran lower on positive affect and higher on negative affect throughout."

**Issue B. Headline uses causal phrasing for a within-person observational finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Walking more lifts your mood, and your mood gets you walking"
- **Abstract says:** "a credible bidirectional relationship between step count and PA (step count → PA: β = 0.06...; PA → step count: β = .07...)"
- **Problem:** "Lifts" and "gets you walking" assert causation from temporally ordered within-person associations with betas of 0.06–0.07. The authors themselves only go as far as "may help improve daily emotional experiences."
- **Suggested fix:** "More steps track with better mood a few hours later — and better mood with more steps — but screen time only pushes one way"

**Issue C. Nationality of cohort not stated in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Dutch cohort"
- **Abstract says:** Author affiliations are Erasmus MC (Rotterdam) and Tilburg University, but the abstract never states where participants were recruited.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. Plausible given the affiliations and the bipolar-offspring design, but it should be confirmed before it appears in a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sample almost certainly Dutch (Erasmus MC-led) — confirm recruitment site from full text."

---

### Study 4: Brain blood flow is lowest in bipolar disorder with psychosis — and higher flow tracks worse symptoms
**PMID:** 42779463 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

Sample sizes (2,412 SZ / 2,278 SAD / 158 BP / 401 NC), 60 regions, d = −0.259 for BP, hypoperfusion in 25 regions, the within-patient positive correlation with psychotic symptoms, and the right superior temporal sulcus finding are all accurate. The caveats are strong. One pitch-level claim, however, contradicts the abstract.

**Issue A. Pitch claims biotypes outperformed diagnosis — the abstract shows the opposite ordering** — Severity: Major

- **As written:** "Diagnosis by category barely predicted brain perfusion; a 'biotype' derived from neurophysiology did."
- **Abstract says:** "Compared to NC, patient groups showed significantly lower total gray matter CBF (PSD: Cohen's d=-0.124, p-adjusted=0.037; BP: d=-0.259, p-adjusted=0.004; the most severe biotype, Biotype 1: d=-0.222, p-adjusted=0.006)."
- **Problem:** Both diagnostic categories and the biotype showed significant hypoperfusion, and the *largest* effect belonged to a DSM diagnostic group (BP, d = −0.259), exceeding Biotype 1 (d = −0.222). The pitch asserts a dissociation the data do not show, and it contradicts the very next sentence of the digest, which correctly notes the bipolar group had the largest deficit. An editor sold this hook would find the paper doesn't deliver it.
- **Suggested fix:** "Both DSM categories and neurophysiology-derived 'biotypes' showed perfusion deficits of similar magnitude — with the bipolar group, usually thought of as the milder end of the psychosis spectrum, showing the largest deficit of all."

**Issue B. Lizano's affiliation as listed in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Paulo Lizano at Beth Israel Deaconess"
- **Abstract says:** "Lizano P(3)(14)" — "(3) Department of Psychiatry, University of Rochester Medical Center, Rochester, NY, USA" and "(14) Department of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA."
- **Problem:** The senior author's listed affiliations on this paper are Rochester and Harvard Medical School; Beth Israel Deaconess is affiliation (1), used by other authors. Worth checking before the contact line runs.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Paulo Lizano (University of Rochester Medical Center / Harvard Medical School)"

### Study 5: Long-acting antipsychotic injections help some people with intellectual disability — and may be harming those prescribed them off-label
**PMID:** 42711066 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Design (self-controlled case series), N=1,675, 2004–2023 window, and the broad direction of both subgroup results are accurately reported, as is the industry COI note.

**Issue A. EPS incidence rate ratio attributed to the wrong analysis** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Among those with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, injections were linked to fewer hospitalizations and dramatically fewer extrapyramidal side effects (IRR 0.34)"
- **Abstract says:** The 0.34 (95% CI 0.23–0.51) is reported in the whole-cohort analysis ("LAIA use was associated with lower risks of ... EPS (0.34, 0.23-0.51)"); the schizophrenia/bipolar subgroup result for EPS is reported as directionally lower, without a figure.
- **Problem:** A number from the overall population is presented as the subgroup effect size.
- **Suggested fix:** "...dramatically fewer extrapyramidal side effects (IRR 0.34 in the full cohort; lower in this subgroup too, though no figure is given)"

**Issue B. Off-label subgroup presented as uniformly worse; two favourable results omitted** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Among those *without* such a diagnosis ... injections were associated with *more* all-cause and somatic hospitalizations and no benefit for behavior problems." / Pitch: "The same drug, the same people, opposite outcomes depending on why it was prescribed."
- **Abstract says:** "among PWID without such diagnoses, LAIA use was associated with higher risks of all-cause hospitalisations, hospitalisations for somatic disorders; **a lower risk of incident all-cause ED visits and hospitalisations for CVDs**, but no significant difference in hospitalisations for behaviour-related problems."
- **Problem:** The off-label result is mixed, not reversed. Dropping the two favourable outcomes makes "harming" and "opposite outcomes" read stronger than the abstract's own careful "raising concern about off-label use."
- **Suggested fix:** "Among those *without* such a diagnosis — where the drugs are prescribed off-label, typically for challenging behaviour — the picture was mixed and less favourable: more all-cause and somatic hospitalisations and no benefit for behaviour problems, though fewer ED visits and cardiovascular admissions." And for the pitch: "The same drug, the same people, a markedly less favourable balance of outcomes when prescribed off-label."

**Issue C. Suggested independent critic is a co-author** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Esther Chan at the University of Hong Kong, and Shoumitro Deb at Imperial College London, a long-standing critic of overprescribing in this population."
- **Abstract says:** Author list includes "Deb S(3)" — "Department of Brain Sciences, Faculty of Medicine, Imperial College London, London, UK."
- **Problem:** Deb is a co-author here. He is still a legitimate interviewee, but the digest should say so rather than framing him as an external critic.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Esther Chan (senior author) and co-author Shoumitro Deb at Imperial College London, a long-standing critic of overprescribing in this population."

### Study 6: The body's own cannabis-like chemicals fall as mania lifts — unless the person uses cannabis
**PMID:** 42735776 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=23 BD I, T0 mania to T1 stabilization, LC-MS/MS, significant AEA and 2-AG decline in non-users, interaction p values, and the null YMRS association are all correct. The "early stage — a hypothesis worth testing" line is a good, honest hedge.

**Issue A. Epub date off by two days** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Published:** 15 December 2026 (epub 16 September 2026)"
- **Abstract says:** "J Affect Disord. 2026 Dec 15;415:122483. ... Epub 2026 Sep 14."
- **Problem:** Wrong epub date; matters only for embargo/priority checks, but it propagates into the citation table.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Published:** 15 December 2026 (epub 14 September 2026)"

**Issue B. "Equivalent clinical improvement" is not established** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "In cannabis users, levels stayed flat despite equivalent clinical improvement"
- **Abstract says:** "cannabis users showed a disrupted trajectory with no significant reduction in eCB tone despite clinical improvement"
- **Problem:** The abstract says both groups improved clinically; it does not report a formal test showing improvement was *equivalent* between groups. "Equivalent" implies a comparison that isn't in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "In cannabis users, levels stayed flat even though they too improved clinically"

**Issue C. Pitch asserts a biochemical "baseline" the study never measured** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Two patients leave the ward looking equally well; only one of them has biochemically returned to baseline."
- **Abstract says:** Plasma AEA and 2-AG were measured at two timepoints in patients only; no healthy comparison group is described, and levels were unrelated to symptom severity.
- **Problem:** With no control sampling and no pre-illness measurement, "returned to baseline" isn't demonstrable — only that levels declined in one group and not the other. The caveat flags the missing control group, but the pitch line still makes the stronger claim.
- **Suggested fix:** "Two patients leave the ward looking equally well; in only one of them has the endocannabinoid signal shifted at all."

*Note (not scored):* Michael Berk is a co-author of this paper, so the "broader bipolar-biomarker view" would come from inside the study team.

### Study 7: People with serious mental illness want AI companions — but only ones built with them, not for them
**PMID:** 42789145 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The body text is a fair rendering of the abstract — concerns about data privacy and misuse, recognized potential for reminders and daily functioning, trust rising with personalization and co-development, worries about overreliance and loss of critical thinking. The equity-interest disclosure is correctly surfaced in both the caveats and the pitch.

**Issue A. Headline overstates qualitative perceptions as a want, and "only" is absolute** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "People with serious mental illness want AI companions — but only ones built with them, not for them"
- **Abstract says:** "participants expressed strong concerns about data privacy and misuse, but also recognized AI's potential to support reminders, mental health, and daily functioning. Trust in AI increased when tools were personalized, human-centered, and co-developed with people who understand lived experiences..."
- **Problem:** Three focus groups establish recognized potential and conditional trust, not a want; and increased trust with co-design is not the same as rejecting anything else. The digest body ("simultaneously enthusiastic and wary") is more accurate than its own headline. A smaller point: "simple companionship" substitutes for the abstract's "mental health" in the list of valued uses — defensible given the title quote, but not lifted from the abstract's own wording.
- **Suggested fix:** "People with serious mental illness are open to AI companions — but trust them more when they're built with them, not for them"

### Study 8: A blood test may show whether lithium is reaching someone's brain
**PMID:** 42742966 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=116, depressive episode in bipolar disorder, PBMC gene expression, the five differentially expressed genes and their directions are all correct, as is the limitation list.

**Issue A. "Why it matters" implies relevance to predicting lithium response, which the study did not assess** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Lithium works well for some people and not others, and there is currently no way to tell early which is which. A peripheral transcriptomic signature that tracks brain white matter would be a step toward a blood-based readout of the drug's biological effect"
- **Abstract says:** "This observation supports the potential usefulness of peripheral transcriptomic signatures to mark the individual biological impact of lithium treatment on the brain."
- **Problem:** No treatment-response outcome appears anywhere in the abstract — this is a cross-sectional comparison of treated vs untreated patients. Opening on the responder-prediction problem invites the reader to assume the signature predicts who benefits, which is a different and much bigger claim than "marks biological impact."
- **Suggested fix:** "Lithium's mechanism remains poorly understood, and there is no way to read its biological effect on the brain short of imaging. A peripheral transcriptomic signature that tracks white matter measures would be a first step toward a blood-based marker of that effect — though it says nothing yet about who will respond."

**Issue B. "Those genes" overstates which genes showed the lithium-specific relationship** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "crucially the relationship between those genes' activity and white matter microstructure existed *only* in lithium-treated patients"
- **Abstract says:** "significant lithium-by-gene expression interactions were observed for SEPTIN11, LEF1-AS1, PLXDC1, and DGKK, indicating that the relationship between gene expression and white matter microstructure differed depending on lithium treatment status."
- **Problem:** Four of the five genes showed interactions (TPPP3 did not), and an interaction means the relationship *differed* by treatment status — not necessarily that it was absent in untreated patients. The abstract's "only in lithium-treated participants" applies to specific gene–diffusion-measure pairings.
- **Suggested fix:** "and for four of the five genes the relationship with white matter microstructure differed depending on whether the patient was on lithium — with the specific associations emerging in lithium-treated patients"

**Issue C. Headline frames a transcriptomic marker as a measure of drug delivery** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A blood test may show whether lithium is reaching someone's brain"
- **Abstract says:** "peripheral transcriptomic signatures to mark the individual biological impact of lithium treatment on the brain"
- **Problem:** "Reaching the brain" suggests a pharmacokinetic question (does the drug get there), which lithium serum monitoring already addresses. The study is about biological impact, not delivery.
- **Suggested fix:** "A blood test may show what lithium is doing to someone's brain"

### Study 9: Half of people with anorexia or bulimia also meet criteria for a personality disorder — but almost nothing is known about why
**PMID:** 42777340 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. All five prevalence figures (49%, 54%, 37%, 47.7%, 9.1%), the 61/213 counts, the credibility grading verdict on risk-factor and outcome estimates, the scope limitation to AN/BN/BED, and the wide CI example all match the abstract. Framing correctly avoids causal claims — indeed the entry's whole point is the absence of credible causal evidence. NS fit of 4 is appropriately modest for a review of reviews.
